subsubtopic: LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT-CALL FOR GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the real tragedies of this Parliament has been its failure to address the very serious unemployment problem in the country. Most Members and most Canadians know that there are fewer Canadians working today than there were four and a half years ago at the time of the last election, even though our population has increased since then. What they are less likely to know and understand is that, in the midst of this unemployment tragedy, the Government has also chosen to cut the training opportunities for Canadians by some 20 per cent. That runs counter to what more progressive and successful nations have been doing.
We hope to see an early election so that more Canadians can be put to work and so that more Canadians can have training opportunities, thus giving more Canadians hope for the future. All that Canadians need to do is turf the Liberals out of office and put the Progressive Conservative Party in office. If they do that, jobs will come.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in many publications and media reports, well meaning but poorly informed writers and journalists have been unjustly critical of the financial input of Canada to NATO. In 1978, at a key meeting of the Alliance, a decision was reached to increase defence spending in real terms by 3 per cent annually.
A table compiled by The Sunday Times of London, and recently published in The Toronto Star, showed the amount each member of NATO contributed in 1983 as compared with the previous year's spending. In summary, the Europeans as a group never reached the 3 per cent benchmark. Belgium and Denmark actually decreased their contributions to NATO in the past year. Canada has increased its spending by 5 per cent.
In response to all of the doubting Thomases who have been critical of Canada's NATO defence spending, Canada in fact is in second place among all NATO members. Only the annual increase of the United States continues to stand ahead of Canada's substantial annual increase in NATO spending.

June 29, 1984

subtopic: FAREWELL MESSAGE FROM MEMBER FOR SASKATOON EAST
FAREWELL MESSAGE FROM MEMBER FOR SASKATOON EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are rumours that there could be a summer election. If that is true, this will be my last time in the House of Commons, and I would like to say a few words of farewell to you, Mr. Speaker, and to my colleagues. I had fully intended to run in the next election and had been nominated on January 28 in my constituency. However, on February 21 I received a message from the Vatican which indicated that under the new code of Canon Law it is no longer possible for me, as a Catholic priest, to continue in active political life. Because I had made a very firm commitment that I was a priest first, and that I would be a priest before, during, and after my political activities, I resigned my nomination on March 1.
I would like to say that it has been a very good, beneficial, and happy experience for me in this House. I appreciate and thank all Members of the House of Commons who have become my friends. I feel that I have been able to state positions clearly which are important concerning international peace and development. I trust that those particular things will be carried on by my colleagues and, in particular, I hope that the person whom I have nominated to represent my constituency, Rev. Colin Clay, who is an Anglican priest, will continue what I have started and will be able to have the same good experiences which I have had in this House.
To one and all, my sincere thanks. It has been a great experience.

subtopic: THREAT TO STEEL INDUSTRY POSED BY POSSIBLE UNITED STATES QUOTAS

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: THREAT TO STEEL INDUSTRY POSED BY POSSIBLE UNITED STATES QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the past three years have been difficult ones for the steel industry in North America, both in Canada and in the United States. In steel producing cities we have seen tens of thousands of steelworkers laid off, many of whom will never return to their jobs. This has been a very serious problem at Algoma Steel, in Sault Ste Marie.
The reduced demand for steel in the United States market, due to the recession and the dumping of cheap imports by countries in South America and Asia, has caused the United States Congress and administration to take legislative action to impose quotas on steel imports in Congress, and to hold hearings of the International Trade Commission.
Canada has always been a fair trading partner with the United States in steel products. Our steel industry, markets, and source of raw materials span across the international
boundary. Canada should be exempt from any quotas imposed by the United States Government. These quotas, if applied to Canada, could result in the loss of as many as 2,000 jobs, many of them in Sault Ste Marie.
The future Prime Minister, who will be sworn in tomorrow, is very aware of this problem as he recently visited Sault Ste Marie and consulted with steel company officials. I would urge him, in the early days of the new administration, to speak with President Reagan in order to ensure that no action will be taken by the United States Government to harm the vital Canadian steel industry further.

subsubtopic: REFORM COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, media reports indicate that the nation should brace itself for a new round of Senate appointments. Will these new appointments be based on the enrichment of the Senate? Will they be based on the merits of the appointees and the contributions they have made to their communities and Canadian society? No, this is Canada. We base Senate appointments on one element, political expediency. If the person who is appointed has any abilities, that is a coincidence, and it more often appears in the case of appointments made of political enemies of the Government rather than of political friends.
What has happened to Senate reform? A joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons studied the problems of the Senate and tried to make recommendations which would lead to the advancement of that body. Those recommendations have been ignored. The most important recommendation was that the Senators should have term appointments. The second most important recommendation was that appointments should reflect the society of Canada. All of this has been ignored in the name of political expediency. Government takes whatever action it chooses. If there is a favoured public servant who has no place to go, he or she is appointed to the Senate. If there is a politician who has stayed too long in office, he is appointed to the Senate.
If we are to have Senate reform it must start now with the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and continue with the new Prime Minister. We cannot have a Chamber that does not reflect Canadian society.

subsubtopic: POLAND-DENIAL OF VISAS TO REUNITE FAMILIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, three people, two men and a woman, are conducting a hunger strike outside the Polish consulate in Toronto. They are endangering their health, and certainly risking their lives. Why are they involved in this very dangerous situation? subsubtopic: IMPACT OF INTEREST RATES ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday the banks increased their prime lending rate to 13 per cent. This came at a time when the Canadian Council on Social Development was finding that one in four families in our country were living below the poverty line. This confirmed earlier findings by Statistics Canada in February that 46 per cent of the unemployed were forced to live at or below the poverty line. Given the fact that there are fewer people working full time in Canada today than when we came here four and a half years ago, I think the House and the country have a right to know from the Minister what rate of interest rates he will tolerate to condemn thousands and thousands more Canadians to unemployment and poverty?

which this Government has passed, there will be no single senior citizen in the future who will be living below the poverty level in this country. This is something which this Government has done, and this is a policy which we have pursued.

speechtext:
On this, his final day, would the Prime Minister grasp the moment to right an historic wrong that has been inflicted on Canadians of Japanese origin? Will the Prime Minister, on this special day, take the time to convey, either on behalf of the Government or on behalf of the Parliament of Canada, a formal apology to Canadian citizens
June 29, 1984

whose rights were so trampled upon in the war years? I think it would be a gesture that would sit well with all Canadians who believe so fundamentally in the sanctity of minority rights.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INTERNED JAPANESE CANADIANS-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TENDER FORMAL APOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the Hon. Leader of the Opposition for his good wishes. I will remember this place with no nostalgia but some kindness, and certainly I have been honoured to serve the people of Canada as best I could in this place for some years. I am very proud of it.
With respect to the matter that he raises, I put it to the Leader of the Opposition that he might want to associate himself with the response of the Government to the recommendations of the Task Force on Visible Minorities when we did express regrets at what had happened to the Canadians of Japanese ancestry on the occasion of the Second World War, and when we announced the setting up of a fund in order to promote racial equality in Canada.
If the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party want to go that far, I think it would be a progressive step, and an encouraging one.
I am not sure what more the Hon. Leader of the Opposition would have in mind when he talks about redressing an historic wrong. There is no way in which we can relive the history of that period. In that sense, we cannot redress what was done. We can express regret collectively, as we have done.
If the Hon. Leader of the Opposition intends going further and indemnifying individual Canadians with sums of money, I think he should make it clear. I know that there is a fair amount of confusion in that. I would have respect for him if he suggested that, and made some provision for the many millions of dollars that would be involved, but the sum of money is not the main question. The main question is how many other historic wrongs have to be righted.
Even today we know that there are people living in Manitoba who have been deprived of their constitutional right since 1890, and who are deprived of a very real freedom of expression in that province. It is not of the same material order as the deprivation that the Japanese Canadians suffered after the war, but I think a deprivation of the spirit of a freedom is also worth some redress. Yet this Government has never suggested that they be given money. We have just suggested that we right the wrong which has been perpetrated in these recent months by a Conservative Government in Manitoba. I know that the Leader of the Opposition shares the regret that we on this side have for that. I just hope that his fellow Tories, if they are so anxious to right wrongs in the case of Japanese Canadians, will think of these wrongs and will do something to right them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brian Mulroney (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have another question for the Prime Minister on this his last day. We are talking about a specific problem, and there is a world of difference between a regret and a formal apology. Canadians of Japanese origin had their rights trampled upon. The reputation of this country was besmirched. All I am asking the Prime Minister today is to acknowledge the fact that this country, this Government, this Parliament, was wrong, and to convey our deep and genuine apologies to the Japanese Canadians, and in so doing tell all visible minorities in this country that this kind of heinous action will never again take place in Canada and, if it does, that we will have the nerve and the courage to stand up and apologize for it and deal with it honourably.
Hear, hear!

That is all I am asking the Prime Minister. I am not trying to cast aspersions or blame. There is enough blame in our history to go around for all of us, Mr. Speaker. I am pointing out to the Prime Minister on his last day that there is a specific problem, and I am asking him if he will rise to the occasion and convey, on behalf of the Government of Canada, a genuine apology to Canadian citizens who were so badly done by. This does not preclude action in other areas in the future.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM CIVIL AND COMMERCIAL JUDGMENTS CONVENTION ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is appropriate to put on the record the purpose of this Bill, not to delay proceedings but in order to provide a written statement as to its purpose.
The Convention between Canada and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland providing for the reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters was signed in Ottawa on April 24, 1984. This Convention codifies the existing principles for recognition of judgments in Canada and the United Kingdom and also simplifies the procedures in this area. The Bill extends the application of the Convention to judgments rendered by the Federal Court.
The main reason for concluding this Convention was the imminent accession by the United Kingdom to a European Convention on the enforcement of judgments. The European Convention provides for the enforcement of judgments of other European states, including some which would not otherwise have been recognized by the United Kingdom courts because they were based on challengeable, frequently qualified as exorbitant bases of jurisdiction.
The European Convention, however, contains a provision which enables the United Kingdom to declare that it will not recognize or enforce any judgment based on exorbitant
June 29, 1984

grounds of jurisdiction given against a party that is domiciled or habitually resident in a specified non-European state. I refer the House to Article 9 of the proposed Canada-United Kingdom Convention whereby the United Kingdom undertakes to make such a declaration.
Before Canada can ratify this Convention, both federal and provincial legislation must be adopted. Almost all of the provinces have undertaken to adopt the necessary legislation. I can advise the House that this has already been done in Ontario and Nova Scotia. Article 12 of the proposed Convention enables Canada to ratify and expand the application of the Convention to specific provinces, not necessarily all provinces.
Since it is expected that the European Convention will come into force in January, 1985, it is very important that the Bill be granted speedy passage to ensure that Canadian assets in the United Kingdom will be protected against claims and judgments which, but for the European Convention, would not be recognized in the United Kingdom.

I might just add in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, since this is probably the last occasion on which I will be speaking in this House, that I have enjoyed very much my 16 years here. I have enjoyed them not only because of the contact I have had with my colleagues in my own Party, but because of the warm, friendly and co-operative relations I have had with Hon. Members of the two other Parties. I would like to thank them for their co-operation and to say that I will keep a very close and friendly eye on proceedings in this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments this Bill is making to the Public Service Superannuation Act are required to confirm the past and future super annuation status of employees of Members of Parliament, many of whom have been participating in the PSSA without clear legislative authority for a number of years. This became apparent only very recently when legal opinions were provided by the Department of Justice and the law branches of the House of Commons and the Senate. In addition to the constituency and Ottawa staff of MPs, the amendments apply to employees of Speakers of both Houses, Government Leaders of both Houses, Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses, staff of the official residences and other similar employees.
The proposed Bill deems the employees of Members of Parliament to be employed in the Senate or House of Commons, whichever is appropriate, for purposes of participation in the PSSA. The Bill also provides that other categories of employees engaged in parliamentary business, paid out of monies appropriated by Parliament for use by the Senate or the House of Commons, can be brought under the Act by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Speaker of the House or the Senate. This regulation-making power can be used for employees such as House of Commons research staff who are in effect working for political Parties but who have been participating in the PSSA In the past and whose coverage we are asking Parliament to ratify.
The Bill provides that coverage will be extended to all present and future employees of Members of Parliament and other categories named by regulation from the date the Bill comes into force. In so far as the past is concerned, employees and retired employees who actually made contributions to the superannuation account will have their coverage and benefits ratified. Existing employees who did not actually contribute prior to the coming into force of the amendment will be given a one-year period to elect to count their prior service and pay for it on the basis of their salaries during the periods in question. This places them on an equivalent basis to those who made contributions in the past.
In conclusion, these amendments are urgently needed to remedy a past legislative oversight which has only recently become apparent, and to protect the promised benefits of the employees in question. There are other outstanding pension issues, but I want to confirm that I have begun consultations with my advisory committee on the Public Service Superannuation Act on the reform of Public Service pension plans and I hope that before too long there will be some conclusions to be brought forward in that regard. In the meantime, there is an urgent situation which I ask the House to remedy through passage of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, we indeed will give speedy passage to Bill C-54. However, I want to spend a few moments talking about it and some of the other things mentioned by the Minister.
When I first realized that some Members' staff had been told they would not receive the pension benefits they understood they should receive under the Public Service Superannuation Act, I was horrified and brought it to the Minister's attention in committee. I was glad to hear him say that there were negotiations going on and two things would happen. One, that the Bill would be brought forward and, two, that the people in question would be dealt with as though the Bill had been in place.
That is only fair; after all, all of us in this House rely so very heavily on our staff. Some of the things we ask them to do by way of long hours and overtime pay deserve to be paid for somewhere along the way, and these benefits that they have paid for are surely a very small way of doing that. It is fair to say that Mr. Speaker and his predecessor, Madam Sauve, have spent a great deal of time putting in place the benefits that

some of us felt for a long time were due our staff. Through their direction to the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services, this and a number of other items are finally coming to pass.
Members know that they will receive in the next few days a comprehensive change in policy with regard to staff benefits and salaries. Finally, we will by August 4 be in a position to pay some of our senior staff a remuneration that comes somewhere close to the work they perform. In the past, there have had to be of necessity all kinds of funny little deals to help us keep top level staff. We will now have, as a result of the letter dated yesterday from the Speaker's office, a long list of changes that will allow us not only to pay them better but also to provide more benefits. To have had this held up would have been unthinkable.
Before I sit down I would like to pay some credit to some of the people who have been directly responsible under Speaker Francis and Speaker Sauve for the implementation of these various changes. I appreciate that in this particular case it was the staff of the Treasury Board who were responsible for these changes, but other changes having to do with salaries have been put in place by the Administrator, Mr. Arthur Silverman, and some of his senior staff. I think it is a credit to the two Speakers that they have had the courage of their convictions to have in place a new administration which, granted, has not always been popular. At least it has had the work of the Members of Parliament in mind at all times and has put in place for the Members' staffs benefits that are relative to their workloads.
We hear repeated rumours that there may be an election this summer. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you would not want either to qualify or deny that suggestion, even if you could, which I doubt you can. If indeed there is an election this summer, the Speaker's chair will, of course, by vacant. I would like to put on record a word of credit to the current holder of the Chair and his predecessor for those things which they have put in place for our staffs over the past years. In doing so, I pay credit to his staff, the administration of the House of Commons.
I cannot add an awful lot to the Bill. We will see this Bill receive third reading and, I assume, Royal Assent later today. We look forward to having these benefits in place for our staffs.

Mr. Speaker, I want to add something to what was said by the Member who preceded me. It never ceases to amaze me how things can slip by for such long periods of time without anyone ever noticing them. I am pleased to see that this has been caught and that those who may well have suffered are going to be taken care of by the legislation and the retroactive feature.
However, this is not all that needs to be done, not by a long shot. Within the operation of the House of Commons as it affects Members' staffs, there is a great deal of work which
Public Service Superannuation Act must be done quickly. I know that I would have the concurrence of the Conservative spokesman in saying that there was some legislation proposed to the House of Commons not so long ago which would have afforded Members' staffs the opportunity to transfer into the Public Service if, as and when they found it necessary to do so as a result of the Member having been defeated. On behalf of my colleagues I had hoped that that legislation would have been forthcoming today too.
For far too long the staff of Members have been treated as second-class citizens in terms of the way in which they have provided for as a result of decisions made, not by the Management and Members' Services Committee, but by the Commissioners of Internal Economy. The Commissioners of Internal Economy do not seem to appreciate the important function of the staffs of Members of Parliament, the increased responsibility that Members' staffs have had to assume and the additional workload which has resulted naturally from the greater degree of public exposure of Parliament and Members and the considerably more complex nature of the work that we do. Members' staffs have been asked to assume responsibilities which I dare say, and I hope I am not offending anyone, would have been unthought of ten or fifteen years ago.
Keeping that in mind, it is important that we address the legitimate requests and matters that affect the day to day operations of Members' offices and the way in which staffs are remunerated and given the opportunity to have a sense of permanency. My good friend and colleague made reference to the issue of now being able to pay Members' staffs at a level higher than we had been allowed to up until now. Unfortunately, we do not have the money to do it. That poses a problem for us. Raising the allowable level but not raising the amounts available for the Members to enable them to pay people at the upper levels is an issue which must be addressed. It strikes me as more than passing strange that we see that kind of proposal come forward from the Commissioners of Internal Economy.
I do wonder at the new direction which has been offered through the Management and Members' Services Committee, but often at the behest of the Commissioners. I am concerned that we are, on the one hand, affording an opportunity for a greater level of benefit or, in the case of this legislation, reinforcing or putting into law that which we always believed was the law in any event. While we are doing that, on the other side of the coin we are reducing the benefits that Members' staffs are to be entitled to. I believe there must be an opportunity for a review of that before it goes too far.
In keeping with that I would like to suggest that matters such as this are in fact properly before the Commissioners of Internal Economy. However, the make-up of the board of commissioners is wrong. While it is clearly the responsibility of the Commissioners of Internal Economy to pass judgments on matters such as this, it is well past time that the Opposition should be represented on the board of the Commissioners of Internal Economy. There must be representation there from other than the Cabinet. The matters which are dealt with by that board, such as this matter, affect every single Member of

They are matters of policy of the House of Commons and if they are to be dealt with fairly and properly, ordinary Members of Parliament must be represented and must make direct representations when the matters are being discussed. That is the case in Ontario. During my time in the legislature of the Province of Ontario, I sat on the board of internal economy. We were able to come to agreement without embarrassing the Government, but also without denying members and their staffs adequate and proper compensation and representation.
Having said those things, Mr. Speaker, perhaps straying ever so slightly from the pith and substance of this legislation, I think that this step, though necessary, is a very tiny step. I think I have the support of all Members in saying that it is time we got together to solve the problems which affect our staff.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take up too much time. I may have only one or two comments to make with respect to this legislation. This Bill and many other items of legislation we have attempted to deal with expeditiously. Basically, I want to say that if the Minister who is responsible for this legislation does not find it convenient or does not have the time to appear here to guide this legislation through, it makes it difficult for us to deal with these matters in a manner which is befitting the importance of the legislation. While the Bill to establish a national park on the Mingan Archipelago is a very thin Bill, it is an important Bill. I am just sorry that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia) who is responsible for Parks Canada is not here. I would have hoped that he would be here to sponsor his own legislation.
Of course, we are prepared to allow the Bill to go through all stages. It demonstrates again that we are co-operative in
terms of putting legislation through and that we attempt to assist the Government in its legislative agenda in many ways.
I simply rise to say that, in supporting this Bill, I am sorry the Minister of the Environment is not here to conduct this legislation on his own. I would hope that during the course of the afternoon the Ministers responsible for other bills that are coming forward will be here to deal with them and will be able to answer questions in the event that such questions are forthcoming in the Committee of the Whole.
Having said that, I will resume my seat and hope that in the last moments of this trimester the message that has been given has been received.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two things to say on the subject. First, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia) is returning to Ottawa from Europe where he attended the acid rain meetings. This was well known by my colleagues in the Opposition.
I was informed that an agreement had been reached to let this Bill go through all stages without debate, but obviously it was not a firm agreement. If the Hon. Member does not want the Bill to go through without the Minister present, then the Bill will not go through because the Minister will not be back on time. However, his Parliamentary Secretary is here. He is an excellent Parliamentary Secretary who is prepared to speak. We were not putting up any speakers because we thought we had an agreement not to speak on this Bill. But the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is here and is prepared to speak on the second reading motion on the Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Denis Ethier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a general understanding that we introduce no speakers but I want to say, as pointed out by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), that it is impossible for the Minister to be here. To show that the work goes on even when our Ministers must be in other countries, we are introducing this Bill in good faith for the Mingan Band. With your kind permission, I will just say a few words of introduction.

The purpose of the Bill I am presenting today, for consideration and approval by the House, is to set aside land for the Mingan Achipelago National Park, which will be the thirtieth in a network of national parks extending from coast to coast. There are national parks in each province and in both territories. We are proud of this system, which is the best in the world, and it gives me great pleasure to present this Bill and to ask the House to join me in setting aside one of the most beautiful spots in this country for the enjoyment of all Canadians.
National parks were created so that Canadians would always have access to places that reflect the natural splendor and serenity of this vast country of ours. These parks have been set aside for the benefit, education and enjoyment of Canadians. Each national park protects representative exam-
June 29, 1984

pies of fauna, flora and also natural areas of outstanding scenic interest. They contain the natural heritage of all Canadians.
The national parks system covers thirty-nine natural regions across Canada. At the present time, only two of the eleven regions in Quebec are part of the system. There are a number of regions missing, one of these being the eastern part of the St. Lawrence lowlands which includes the Mingan Archipelago.
The Mingan Archipelago consists of twenty-five islands spread out over a distance of approximately fifty miles along the North Shore of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, from lie aux Perroquets in the west, to lie Sainte Genevieve in the east. The proposal to reserve the Archipelago for a national park would be a worthy prelude to the festivities planned for the national parks centennial in 1985.
Fossil deposits, flower-pot formations, rare plants and colonies of sea birds in the Archipelago have for many years attracted the attention of naturalists, conservationists and tourists. By reserving the territory of the Archipelago for a national park, it will be possible to safeguard these natural resources. There will also be a positive impact on the economy of the North Shore, where the unemployment rate is over 20 per cent. Expenditures earmarked for salaries of Parks Canada employees and for park operations will act as an immediate stimulus to the regional economy. Within ten years or so, the Archipelago will be able to receive about 30,000 visitors annually, compared to a total of 12,000 last year, and the local population will benefit from what is spent by park visitors. Finally, payment of grants in lieu of taxes for the lands acquired in order to create a national park will further enhance the economic benefits.
Why would Parks Canada want to reserve the lands of the Mingan Archipelago for a national park, instead of just creating a park? The Mingan Archipelago lies within a territory that is the subject of land claims by the Attikamek-Montag-nais Council. The Mingan Band has already agreed in principle to this Bill. Establishing a park reserve guarantees that creation of the national park cannot be definitive until native land claims have been settled. Any right, title or interest of native peoples included in a claim will be recognized within the limits of the national park. Visitors will therefore be able to visit the Archipelago, and go hiking and camping and on guided tours, depending on the fragility of the environment.
The Mingan Archipelago will be the thirtieth national park and a new and very substantial asset to a national parks system that already has an international reputation. In concluding, I again wish to thank the Opposition parties for agreeing to limit debate to one speaker per Party.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join the Parliamentary Secretary in thanking the Department of the Environment, and the two Ministers who were respon-
Mingan Archipelago National Park Act sible for Environment Canada and Parks Canada, for the tremendous work they have done to make one of the major natural resources of the North Shore, namely, its coastal region, into a national park. Mr. Speaker, I also wish to thank Parks Canada officials for their exceptional achievement in creating this park. At this stage, I think the park is a major step for the North Shore towards economic diversification.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would like to thank the chiefs of the Mingan Band for their contribution and their support for reserving the lands for this park. Throughout the process, we intend to take into consideration native rights and traditions that must be respected. We have promised them that nothing will be done without their permission, so that native traditions will indeed be respected. Mr. Speaker, this is a red-letter day for the North Shore, and since today is the last day of this session, I also wish to thank the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who visited Natashquan on May 4, 1982, and flew over the Mingan islands. It was then that we thought of creating this national park, a place where Canadians could find knowledge and repose and enjoy the splendors of this part of Canada and Eastern Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, may I add a
few comments to those already made regarding Bill C-53 which will see the creation of a new national park. It is our understanding that this park is ready to go and the Government has financing for it. It will provide valuable jobs in an area where unemployment is regrettably very high.
In terms of the philosophy and concept of the park, it is very clear that we have areas right across Canada that are represented by national parks. One year from now we will be having the 100th anniversary of our national parks system. It will be good to have Mingan National Park included at this time so it can be part of the celebrations and be included in the representation we have of national parks across Canada.
There are other areas in Canada, such as South Moresby and the Bruce Peninsula, that can be similarly considered in their own way to represent for the people living in those areas the national parks system. We are happy to co-operate with the Minister on this Bill. We regret the Bill was brought forward at such a late date and under such constrained circumstances, which means it cannot receive the full consideration that I believe a Bill like this should have. Be that as it may, we are co-operating and are happy to see it go forward.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief. The terms of the tax conventions embodied in Bill S-11 are similar, at least in broad outline, to those in Bill S-14, the Bill concerning a tax convention with the United States which was adopted in the House a few days ago.
The eight tax conventions covered by Bill S-ll follow the general pattern of similar tax conventions approved by Parliament in the past. The convention with Sweden, when in force, will replace the existing agreements signed in 1951. I might add that when these eight conventions are ratified, the number of Canadian tax treaties in force with other countries, will increase from 32 to 39.
How can you add 8 to 32 and arrive at 39?

I am sorry, I meant to say seven. The conventions follow the normal practices with regard to such treaties between sovereign nations. They cover such matters as capital gains and non-discrimination. Provision is made in several of the conventions for the taxation of foreign teachers in Canada. The pensions paid to residents are included in this Bill. The standard provision for double taxation relief is also

incorporated in each of the tax conventions under consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in my remarks on Bill S-l 1. As we know, it was passed in the Senate on May 24 after having had reasonable examination in the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce. It is some 175 pages in length and it is about as exciting as watching paint dry. However, it is one of those things which have to be done.
We do not want to hear about what you do in your spare time.

It covers a whole series of taxation matters between Canada and Tunisia, Bangladesh, Cameroon, Sri Lanka, Kenya, Egypt, the Ivory Coast and Sweden. It will allow for commercial and personal financial matters to proceed in an orderly manner without double taxation. Of course, it deals with matters of taxation on income and capital.
For example, it defines fiscal domicile where a person has a residence in both countries, to be determined by a set of rules which have been established as a result of negotiations between our Government and the governments of the contracting countries. Also there is a provision to determine permanent establishments. That is the term used where a business is carried on in two countries. Also it defines place of management, branch, office, factory, workshop, mine, quarry, et cetera. We now have ground rules by which to determine all these matters.
As well it deals with matters pertaining to shipping and air transport, matters relating to profits, dividends, capital gains, interest income, royalties, directors' fees, compensation to artists and athletes, teachers' salaries, students' income where they attend school and work in one of the contracting countries, as well as miscellaneous income. Of course, it will assist in the orderly commercial arrangements between Canada and those other countries.
As the Minister indicated, we now have agreements of this nature with 39 different countries. It helps us in our commercial relations with those countries to know that we have a taxation regime which can be defined by both sides and will allow standard, normal business practice to carry on between the contracting countries.
That is about all I have to say. I understand there is a disposition to have the Bill considered in Committee of the Whole today.

Mr. Speaker, I found interesting the analogy of the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) in terms of the excitement of reading this particular legislation. I have never been in the position of watching paint dry, unlike my colleague. I suspect he is right; I cannot verify it.
As the Hon. Member said, the legislation has gone through the Senate. As is my normal practice, I sat and read assiduously through all the Senate committee proceedings to ensure that
Income Tax Conventions
the matters had been dealt with properly and that its deliberations were in fact in keeping with the kinds of things we would have done here. It may well be that we have finally found a use for the Senate. Perhaps this is an appropriate use to which the Senate can be put on matters such as this, as important as they are but less political in nature.
In any event, like the Official Opposition we will facilitate the passage of these seven agreements reached between our Government and the governments of those foreign jurisdictions.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister referred rather briefly in his comments to the non-discrimination clauses of the conventions, copies of which are part and parcel of the Bill. Indeed they mirror the non-discrimination clauses in Bill S-l4 which the House has already passed. I wonder whether the House is fully aware of the fact that the Income Tax Act, as it currently stands, establishes a small business deduction based upon discrimination. One ground for the discrimination is not whether corporations are only small but whether they are Canadian controlled.
Since these conventions are substantially the same, I should like to examine for the purposes of demonstration paragraph 3 of Article VI of the convention with Tunisia. It is interesting to note that the taxation on a permanent establishment which an enterprise of a contracting state has in the other contracting state shall not be less favourably levied in that other state than the taxation levied on enterprises in the other state carrying on the same activities.
When we intend to amend the Income Tax Act, it would be so nice for the Income Tax Act to be amended in the House instead of its being amended as a consequence of a Bill originally introduced in the Senate being given speedy passage in this House. I pause to note that despite the fact the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) was urged to bring in the Bill amending the Income Tax Act, which should have followed his Budget of February 15, he has not done so.
This series of treaties will in effect overrule any provisions of the local law. We amend the provisions of the Income Tax Act by passing this statute which will be interpreted by the courts as having primacy over the provisions of the income tax legislation.
I wonder whether the Minister of Finance, in projecting his revenues from those corporations carrying on business in Canada with a small business deduction limit which may be the same as Canadian-controlled corporations, whereas the shareholders of those corporations are foreign, is relying upon the receipt of income from those corporations in excess of the amounts he will receive once this Bill is passed.
Too little regard has been paid in the dying moments of this session and possibly the dying moments of this Parliament to the implications that these tax conventions will have upon revenue. It is quite permissible if you seek to lower taxation in Canada for both Canadian controlled and non-Canadian con-

June 29, 1984
Income Tax Conventions
trolled corporations to do so as long as you recognize what you are doing. My great fear is that this Government, through its negotiators, has prepared some conventions which will have the effect of tying the hands of whatever Minister of Finance we have in Canada because we have eliminated the possibility of continuing the special small business deduction which is allowable to Canadian controlled private corporations.
I would like to remark for a moment upon the exchange of information program that this Government, in the event that this Bill passes, may be obliged to undertake. In looking at the first convention, the one with Tunisia to which reference has been made, the provision for the exchange of information is not as extensive as that contained in Bill S-14 and the attached tax convention between Canada and the United States. It is, nevertheless, a remarkable departure from the way in which tax conventions hitherto have functioned.
I am particularly concerned about the potential of providing information to foreign tax authorities and, accordingly, to the governments of foreign states with respect to the business activities of Canadian corporations and in particular trade secrets of Canadian corporations which may be made available to foreign jurisdictions. In the case of Bill S-14, we not only provide for depositions that would be taken in Canada for the benefit of a foreign country, we also provide for the collection of taxes imposed by a foreign jurisdiction. I submit that step is a remarkable departure from the way in which current tax conventions have operated. It would have been nice had the Minister, when he explained the provisions of some of these Bills, specifically noted the remarkable departure that we have been confronted with as a consequence of the changes in the tax conventions. He has not done that, save and except to make some reference to the non-discrimination clauses which, as I said, have a detrimental effect upon the way in which our current Income Tax Act functions.

On Clauses 2 to 27-

Mr. Chairman, I indicated in the brief remarks I made with respect to the Bill that I did not know whether the Minister was cognizant of the implications of what he referred to as the non-discrimination effect of this legislation. Would the Minister comment on that?

Mr. Chairman, under the conventions, discrimination on the basis of nationality is prohibited, thereby ensuring nationals of a country equal treatment with nationals of the other country is the same circumstances. However, that does not prevent a country from providing fiscal incentives; for example, a small business deduction on the basis of the residence of the taxpayer. I would only add that the convention with the Ivory Coast does not contain an article of non-discrimination and consequently the rules of the domestic legislation will there apply.

Mr. Chairman, it may well be that we will ultimately determine the difference between the Minister and myself when we have a variety of tax cases in front of us, which I suspect will ultimately go to the Supreme Court of Canada to determine whether the Minister is correct or I am correct. Reference has already been made to paragraph 3 of Article 23. It is very clear that the taxation on a permanent establishment which an enterprise of a contracting state has in the other contracting state shall not be less favourably levied in that other state than the taxation levied on the enterprise in that other state carrying on the same activities.
The Minister suggested that what the small business deduction amounts to is a special incentive. Of course, it is not a special incentive; it is a provision of general application that will apply to all corporations provided they meet the financial requirements entitling them to that deduction. It is very clear that the measure of taxation imposed against anyone is an end product of an amount calculated by determining what one's taxable income is and what is the rate of tax applied against that taxable income.
What this clause and all non-discrimination clauses will do when applied specifically to permanent establishments is make it obligatory for the Government to allow all foreign corporations, which in fact meet the financial guidelines of our Income Tax Act, to be entitled to the same small business deduction, because that deduction is available in the event that you meet certain standards. One of the standards happens to be whether you are Canadian controlled; another is whether you have met certain fiscal requirements. If foreign-controlled corporations meet those fiscal requirements, I submit we are discriminating against those foreign corporations, thereby breaching the provisions of the convention Canada is to enter into.
The Minister knows the effect of a court judgment where there is a clash or a conflict between convention provisions and the provisions of the Income Tax Act; the convention provisions apply.

East): Mr. Speaker, I was going to propose two amendments at the report stage, but unfortunately I believe the rules require some improvement, because I feel that my rights have been denied in not being able to make those amendments. In any case, I will state what I intended to do now at third reading. While I completely support those parts of this Bill which would abolish discrimination against Indian women, and I have supported the abolition of Section 12(1 )(b) and others for many years, I do not hold the same position with respect to some of the other clauses in the Bill, in particular, those clauses which deal with the reinstatement of those persons who lost their status in past years. I firmly believe there has to be reinstatement provisions. We have to reinstate those people who have lost their status. However, the clauses in this Bill for reinstatement are extremely inadequate and many witnesses before the standing committee which met in the last couple of days gave evidence of that.
Once again, by passing sections of the law on such sensitive measures which affect Indian people, we are acting like a colonial institution. We are a white man's Parliament, for the most part, imposing our views on Indian people in a very paternalistic way. I would like to point out those parts of the Bill which are inadequate and which have been highlighted by the Assembly of First Nations and by the Native Women's Association of Canada.
First, the Bill does not permit the reinstatement of all Indian citizens who were previously denied registration. Because reinstatement is arbitrarily cut off at half of the second generation, the Bill perpetuates the very discrimination which it is supposed to terminate. I was going to propose an amendment which would have allowed the reinstatement of more people, basically a great many more people who had lost their status but who were still able to trace their lines to certain Indian

bands. That is the first area in which the Bill is inadequate and one area I wanted to amend.

I myself, along with other Hon. Members of this House, have sat for a year and a half on the Indian self-government committee in which we proposed that there be a bilateral relationship between the Canadian Government and the Indian nations in this country. We also proposed that Indian nations should have the right to determine their own citizenship.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe we should indicate that the procedural mish-mash which we have just seen in the House is typical of the entire handling of this Bill. It should have been possible on a day like this when we are finally getting rid of Section 12(1)(6) to feel good about doing something positive for Indian people. Instead, that feeling has been turned to dust and ashes in the mouth of every Hon. Member who sat on that committee. Bill C-47, an Act to amend the Indian Act, and to remove discrimination, also does other things to Indian people, with which we are not at all happy. It is not possible for any Hon. Member in this House, nor for the Minister for that matter, to rise and make any kind of a self-congratulatory speech that at long last we are ending this injustice, because we cannot congratulate ourselves on what is happening. We all know the history of Section 12(1)(6) and the way in which it
has become in the Indian Act a symbol of sexism, racism and assimilation.
It is a symbol of sexism because through it a woman derives her status from her husband. The emphasis throughout the Indian Act is on the male line. It is racist in its implication that Indians are somehow lower on the scale of humanity and that by marrying a non-Indian, an Indian woman is supposed somehow to have risen on the scale of humanity and thus no longer to have Indian status. And, of course, just the opposite was true for a non-Indian woman who married an Indian male so that this non-Indian woman acquired Indian status. This racist assumption runs through the entire Indian Act.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, Section 12(1)(6) is typical and symbolic of the assimilationist aspects of the entire Indian Act because, like other sections of that Act, it was designed to reduce the number of status Indian people. One of the forerunners of the present Indian Act was entitled "An Act for the gradual enfranchisement of the Indians", and it is interesting that in 1920, when the Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Duncan Campbell Scott, was testifying at a special committee of the House of Commons, he said, and I quote:
I want to get rid of the Indian problem. I do not think as a matter of fact, that this country ought to continuously protect a class of people who are able to stand alone. That is my whole point. I do not want to pass into the citizens' class people who are paupers. This is not the intention of the Bill. But after one hundred years, after being in close contact with civilization it is enervating to the individual or to a band to continue in that state of tutelage, when he or they are able to take their position as British citizens or Canadian citizens, to support themselves, and stand alone. That has been the whole purpose of Indian education and advancement since the earliest times. One of the very earliest enactments was to provide for the enfranchisement of the Indian. So it is written in our law that the Indian was eventually to become enfranchised.
-our object is to continue until there is not a single Indian in Canada that has not been absorbed into the body politic and there is no Indian question, and no Indian Department, that is the whole object of this Bill.
That was said in 1920, Mr. Speaker. Section 12(l)(b), by denying Indian status to Indian women who married non-Indians, was just one aspect of that assimilationist policy. Section 12(l)(b) has split Indian communities and Indian families. We heard testimony countless times, not only during the hearings which we held with regard to Bill C-47 but also in the subcommittee and the special committee on Indian self-government. We heard testimony from a great many Indian leaders that they wanted to end this division. They wanted their sisters and their daughters back in the community. Section 12(1 )(b) and the other sexist sections on the Indian Act were an imposition on the Indian people by the Government, the non-Indian Government. It was not an Indian designed proposal at all.
[DOT] (MIO)
It is important to recognize that Section 12(l)(b) and others have hurt Indian women in at least three basic ways. Most obvious, it resulted in a loss of status for those Indian women who married non-Indians. Secondly, an important number of Indian women gave up a relationship that would have led to marriage because they did not want to lose their status. As they were growing up, it was emphasized to them that if they

June 29, 1984

married a non-Indian they would lose that special and very important status. That is regrettable. There is a third group of Indian women who did not wish to give up a relationship or their status and so they entered into a common-law relationship, had children, but they would very likely have wished to have had their marriage regularized in some way. This section has penalized Indian women and their communities in countless ways, and at long last it is being repealed. This is something desired by all parties and the majority of Indian people.
However, we cannot be self-congratulatory because of the way we are dealing with this Bill. This end of discrimination was supposed to have been a major commitment on the part of this Government and the previous Government, yet we had to wait four years until the very last month of this Parliament. The Bill was tabled only two weeks ago and we only had three or four days to deal with it in committee. This, in spite of repeated requests to table the Bill early so that there would be adequate time to study it, hear from Indian people and make sure it was as acceptable as possible to the Indian people. The committee had to deal with it in a very rushed atmosphere, which did not do justice to the Act. I think most members of the committee question whether we are really doing justice to the Indian people.
There was limited time for testimony from Indian people and even less time for dealing with our amendments. In effect, we had time for one shot at acceptable amendments. When they came back and we wanted to make further changes it was too late. It is that kind of rushed atmosphere that we are dealing with here this afternoon. The committee was put in an impossible position by the Government. Either we had to leave Section 12(1 )(b) on the books, which would deny justice to Indian women, or we had to accept the implicit assumption of this Bill that Indians somehow could not be trusted to do justice to their own people. We are in a situation where non-Indians, all of us here, are making decisions for Indian people and their communities.
The Trudeau years began with the promise of participatory democracy and are ending with this kind of fiasco. I cannot help but contrast the promise of participatory democracy with last night's committee meeting. After the members of the committee had made what was not an easy decision for anyone, there was a request from some of the Indian leaders to make a final statement. Leaders from the Assembly of First Nations and the Native Women's Association of Canada spoke to the committee and acknowledged our hard work. But they indicated that the Bill itself was completely unsatisfactory. The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) indicated some of the ways in which they found this Bill unsatisfactory. I moved an amendment that would have given bands control over residency rights from the reserve for non-Indian spouses, but this was denied.
In 1947, when proposals were made to change the Indian Act, Indian speakers from across Canada representing the Alberta Indian Association, bands from Ontario and the Native Brotherhood of British Columbia all made presenta-
Indian Act
tions suggesting that they were the people who should be looking after their own membership. They knew the needs of their people and they wanted to be able to design membership requirements that would meet the needs of their people. That Government, in its wisdom or lack of it, decided that Indian people should not be trusted with looking after their own membership. It then brought in even more bureaucratic changes to the membership sections, including the notorious double-mother clause. Indian people have continued to suffer because non-Indian people have been making legislation for them. Clause 16(b) of Bill C-52, tabled this past week, recognizes the power of the Indian Government to legislate on applications for membership. Unfortunately, that Bill was tabled too late for any legislative action this year. Again we wonder why it took so long to table it. But the question the Indian people ask is, if they have the power in Bill C-52 to look after their own membership, why is that same power not in Bill C-47? That is a good question and I do not have an answer.
One of the difficulties committee members found in trying to draft amendments was that Department of Justice officials who were there helping us draft the amendments kept saying that whatever we were proposing was contrary to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We had hoped the Charter would have expanded the role of self-determination and autonomy for all people in Canada rather than hemming in the aboriginal peoples as it seems to do. But this kind of attitude on the part of the officials-and perhaps they are accurately reflecting the Charter of Rights and Freedoms-underlines the need for constitutional entrenchment of the aboriginal right to self-government. This was recommended by the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government.
The New Democratic Party gives its consent to the passage of this Bill, but it is a reluctant consent. The elimination of Section 12( 1 )(b) of the Indian Act should have been a cause for rejoicing, but because of the way this Bill has been handled that rejoicing has been turned to ashes in our mouths. We hope that the review process will take a long and detailed look at some of the provisions of this Bill and that a future government will be able to deal with them in a more sensitive frame of mind and over a more extended period of time.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to take part in a historic debate in this Parliament. Canadian women, especially native

June 29, 1984
Indian Act
women, have worked very hard for this day to come. It is regrettable that Parliament did not have adequate time to make a proper study. The committee was pushed. It is not precisely the Bill that we would have liked. Native women are not happy with it. The Assembly of First Nations is not happy with it. The National Action Committee is not happy with it. We would all have liked something a little different from what we have before us. Nonetheless, this is a historic day. A historic injustice to native Canadian women is going to be corrected. That is something to celebrate.
I want to pay tribute to the many native women who have struggled to achieve equality for themselves and their sisters. I think of women like Lavell and Bedard who took cases to the Supreme Court of Canada and were denied justice and equality by the Supreme Court of Canada under the old Bill of Rights. I think of women like Sandra Lovelace who took her case to the United Nations and brought international attention to the disgraceful discrimination which is currently in Section 12(l)(b) of the current Indian Act. I think of the women who have worked for rights for Indian women and for the Native Women's Association of Canada and the various other Canadian women's groups which have supported them. I think very especially of Mary Two-Axe Early who struggled a long time ago. She went before the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. Year after year she has lobbied the Government. She is here in the galleries today. We really must pay tribute to her for the patience, courage and nobility of her struggle. She is a splendid person. She exemplifies what is so important in native Canadian women.
It is due to the quality of people like this that we can rejoice at having this Bill passed today. It means that with their courage, determination, intelligence and commitment to their bands and to their people, native women will be part of the struggle of native people for justice and for a fair part in Canadian society. Women who until now have had to struggle for their rights within their communities can now unite with their communities to work for a better place in Canadian society.
We have the pleasure of being part of a Parliament that is correcting a historic injustice. This is not perfect legislation, but a terrible problem is going to be solved. We can all be very proud that on this last day of Parliament we will leave knowing that we have done good work in changing this historic wrong in Canadian society.
